summary: Annabel Streets argues that many midlifers, the "sandwich generation", end up "parenting" their own parents, and that encouraging older parents to engage with technology, walk daily, socialise, take a multivitamin and eat enough protein can protect their brain and mental health. She draws on studies from the University of Texas, Columbia University and Limerick researcher Dr Eamon Laird. The piece ends with advice that over-50s follow the same habits as "self-parenting" and a list of groups for older people.
one_line: Research-backed advice on helping ageing parents stay mentally and physically healthy through tech use, walking, socialising, multivitamins and protein.
key_facts: Midlifers who parent both children and their own parents are known as the sandwich generation.
A recent University of Texas study of more than 200 elderly adults found that those who engaged with technology had better cognition and memory than non-engaging peers.
Earlier studies found that older people who actively used technology were less likely to get dementia.
Annabel Streets' 84-year-old mother recently joined Instagram, which expanded her mental activity and helped her stay in touch with her grandchildren.
Dr Eamon Laird's study of more than 4,000 older adults found that as little as 20 minutes of daily walking could cut the risk of depression by up to 43%.
Laird says older parents should be urged to walk five days a week, and that depression risk fell in proportion to time spent walking.
Gerontologists believe depression is one of the most common psychiatric disorders among the elderly, with half of all cases going undiagnosed.
Laird recommends vitamin D and B12 supplements, which appear to moderate the chance of depression in older people.

Health coach Susan Saunders parented her mother, who had dementia, while her own daughters were babies, and recommends joining Dementia Research, a nationwide register matching volunteers to research programmes.

A Columbia University study of 2,200 adults aged 60 and over found a multivitamin formulated for older people improved cognition, memory and focus, potentially slowing age-related memory decline by three years.
Laird advises older adults to take at least 1 to 1.5g of protein per kilogram of body weight, from dairy, fish or non-processed meat, to maintain muscle strength and reduce frailty risk.
Streets' guidelines for anyone over 50: engage with something new daily, walk at least 20 minutes daily, socialise regularly, take a senior multivitamin and check protein content of meals.
